utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, and perhaps a special welcome to Mr. Kuzmanovic, who's, well, to say on his feet again is right and, same the time -- Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could I have your assistance. Since we're waiting for the witness, I take it that at a later stage we'll deal with the 92 ter statements. Page 28 of the witness statement says: By 5th of August, 1991, Mrksic who had returned in May 1995, may I take it that this is a typo and that most likely it will be 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the -- and a new Frenki apparently arrives -- Stamatovic often where one would expect Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think he addressed that in the Milosevic trial testimony, Mr. President, he said that Frenki used both names, and he knew him as both Stamatovic and Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have missed that. And you may understand that the waiting the agreement between the parties, I had not read every single page of the many, many pages at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic, I take it. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text will be handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you express yourself in English. Does that mean that you would like to give your testimony in the English language, or would you rather use your native language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer to do it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will first be examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you first please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And right at the outset because you have chosen to speak in English, I need to advise you that we need to control the tempo at which we speak for the benefit of the court reporters and the court interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For example.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. So if you could pause at the end of the question, and I will try to pause at the end of the answer. And I think that will greatly assist the court staff. Mr. Lazarevic, I think the court usher has handed you now a copy of your 1999 statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on or about the 1st of July, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Taking a look through this statement, and looking at the signatures on each page, is this in fact the statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking through the statement, and if I may first take you to several pages. If you could go to page 19 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, the 1999 statement is 65 ter 1D399.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: During your proofing with us yesterday, you wanted to correct something with respect to which intelligence service Mr. Karan worked for. Do you wish to make that correction now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The part of the statement it states that Colonel Karan was a part of the SDB, which is apparent mistake. Sluzba Drzavne Bezbednosti -- he is a military personnel. So he is a part of the KOS which deals with the internal security, vojna drzavne bezbednosti.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So he worked for the SVB and not the SDB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I think there is only one place that I do this. Everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning to page 22, please. On this page you wanted to make a correction regarding the portion of the statement that says Mr. Sarac ordered prisoners to be shot. You wish to add something to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. This is not a statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What -- so that portion of the statement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to 28 of your statement, please. In the first paragraph, it says in the third sentence: "By 5 August 1991, Mrksic, who had returned in May 1995 as commander of the RSK ..." that date 5 August 1991, should that in fact be 5 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On that same page, the statement, at the bottom, says: "I, myself, concocted a story of civilians being massacred by the Muslims which got reported on CNN." Did you wish to correct that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I never made that statement assuming I was never in touch with them. Somebody else from within the building did, But it was attributed to me for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you contend that what was told to CNN was concocted or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I never made that statement, so whether it was a made-up statement by somebody else or something, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I could turn your attention to page 33. At the very top of the page the statement says: "In any event, people were so brainwashed and so terrorised by their government's propaganda that few would have risked staying in Croatia." I believe you told us that you did not use the word "brainwashed" but that you agree that the population was terrorised by its own government's propaganda. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: General statement is correct, apart from word used, "brainwashed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Other than those corrections, is there anything else that needs to be corrected in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you gave this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in July of 1999, were the statements that you gave in this statement true at the time that you made them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions that you were asked then, if I were to ask them in Court today, would your answers be the same subject --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- subject to the corrections that you have made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that exhibit 65 ter 1D399 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, I mean, we don't object to it. I just don't know whether strictly speaking he said that it accurately reflects what he said; that's minor. The other point is that he referred to the hard copy, the one in e-court will be in evidence. We should confirm that the one on the screen is the same. And barring those, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other Defence teams. No objections. Mr. Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I think it's more or less transpired from your answers what is written down reflects what you said at the time, apart from this portion where you said, This is not my statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please repeat the number which does not appear on the transcript, and I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit 1461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1461 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could call up 1D2703, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you recall that you gave testimony in this Tribunal in October 2002 in the case of the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked a series of questions and provided a series of answers to questions asked of you by the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber in that case. Were the answers that you provided at that time true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've had a chance to review the trial transcript. Do the statements -- does the transcript accurately reflect what you told the Court in 2002?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you today in court the same questions that you were asked in court in 2002, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender the excerpts which are in 1D -- sorry. 1D2703 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I see this from your nodding that there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And same is true, I take it, for the Defence teams. It is -- Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1462 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a summary of the witness's testimony. I have provided the summary to the booths and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that you have explained to Mr. Lazarevic what the purpose of reading out the summary, so that the public know what is in your written statement or in the transcript, what is, as a matter of fact, a summary of the evidence you're providing to this Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness Slobodan Lazarevic was a former intellegence officer who worked for Yugoslav army counter-intelligence abroad from 1968 to approximately 1990. In 1991, Mr. Lazarevic became an intelligence officer for the Republika Srpska Krajina. The witness testifies that his job in RSK intelligence was, amongst other things, to obstruct the work of the United Nations peacekeepers and European Union monitors in order to keep them from finding out the truth about Krajina Serb activities. According to the witness "every interpreter working for the UN and the ECMM in the Krajina was reporting back to Serbian intelligence organs." From early 1992 onwards the witness was instructed by his superior to recruit UN and ECMM international personnel as cooperating agents the for the RSK. The witness provided international personnel with money and women. The witness was able to receive intelligence information from ECMM and UN monitors. The witness attended four international peace negotiations as a delegate of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The purpose of these peace negotiations was to try to reach a peaceful settlement of the dispute between Croatia and the RSK. The witness testifies, however, that any time a delegation from the RSK attended a conference abroad, the RSK delegation would have to go to Belgrade at least 24 hours in advance to be briefed by representatives of the Serbian government. Belgrade did not want any settlement of issues that divided the RSK Serbs and the Croatian government. The witness testifies that his delegation was instructed in Belgrade to raise every conceivable procedural and technical problem, just to delay an agreement being reached. Belgrade had given very strict instructions to the delegation that the political side of the delegation was not to reach any agreement on an autonomy plan. Even when it became obvious near the end that the RSK could not survive, Belgrade would still not allow the RSK delegation to negotiate in good faith. Instead the delegation was continuously instructed to obstruct fruitful negotiations and to delay. The witness states that there was a standing policy in the RSK to force Croats from the Krajina. Each corps within the RSK army was expected to have units available to do dirty jobs towards this end. It was tasked with targeting Croat civilians and creating a climate of fear. According to the witness, the existence of the RSK was dependant upon the Serb population believing that they could never live with the Croats and anyone challenging this proposition was seen as a threat to the RSK government. By 1995, life in the Krajina had become even more difficult for people living there. It seemed as if everyone had gone crazy. Every dispute began being settled with guns. The problem was compounded by the total militarization of the population. Every male between the ages of 18 and 65 was mobilized. Everyone was armed and everyone was required by law to be in uniform all the time, whether they were on duty or not. The total militarization and the climate of fear created by the RSK government combined to oppress people, and violence became the norm. Of all Serb losses in the Krajina between 1991 and 1995, the witness estimates that 80 per cent were the result of Serb-on-Serb violence. The night before Operation Storm, a European Union monitor named Bent Jenssen had obtained the HV's plans for attack in Operation Storm and passed those plans to the witness. The witness immediately forwarded this information to the ARSK Main Staff in Knin. During Operation Storm, the witness states that panic set in among the civilian population in Sector North when they realized that there was nothing that could stop Croatian troops. There was a universal feeling that when the HV retook the area, they would be out for revenge after what had happened to the Croats in 1991. The panic was fostered by Belgrade which wanted the Serbs to leave Krajina so they could resettle them in Kosovo and Serb-held areas of Bosnia and eastern Slovenia. It was a well orchestrated plan, and the RSK government and military contributed to the process by intentionally sowing panic among the civilian population. The witness states that the vast majority of Serbs had left well before Croatian forces reached them. During Operation Storm, a number of Serbs shot each other in disputes which arose over vehicles or property as people prepared to flee. The witness says that people were so terrorised by their own RSK government's propaganda that few would have risked staying in Croatia. When the witness arrived Serbia, he saw how the Serbian police was directing RSK refugees to Kosovo. Men from the RSK aged 16 to 65 were arrested in Serbia and sent to Arkan's retraining centre in eastern Slavonia. After retraining, these men were to be sent back to fight against the Croatian army. Mr. President, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, just a few questions about your background. You joined the Yugoslav army counterintelligence service in 1968?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us who Nicola Zimonja was to you, at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nicola Zimonja was the first contact I had with KOS, and we stayed throughout my engagement with KOS as a point of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was he your point of contact throughout your tenure working in KOS up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After 1990, when you joined the RSK, did you have any relationship to Nick Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was Nikola Zimonja in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't really believe that he any appointments as officer of RSK army because he was JNA. But he would come to -- to the field quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would he come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And was he still KOS at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were RSK, ARSK at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Working in the ARSK, how is it -- were you working for Mr. Zimonja as well while you were in the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'd rather like to look at it and say I was working for the Yugoslav government, instead of working for one individual person. But he was my handler, so all the information that I had to supply went through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me make sure we're talking about the same time-period. Between 1991 and 1995, were you working -- did you consider yourself working for the Yugoslav government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but your official title was what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A liaison officer of 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Of the?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So can you tell us why were you presenting yourself publicly as working for the ARSK but privately you considered yourself working for the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was not matter of presenting oneself. The official situation that I was employed as an officer of RSK, it was the one that was maintained so that my access to the international community was made even easier or possible. I could not very well present myself as an officer of JNA at that time, since the JNA officially already withdrew from the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement at page 7 you mention Toso Pajic. Can you tell the Court what your relationship was to Toso Pajic, as well as what he was during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My work with Toso Pajic was on a daily base throughout my stay in Krajina. He was named as a liaison officer for the police of the RSK. He became the minister of interiors later on. He is a career police officer, and yet he worked for the SDB of Serbia all of this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you talk about -- actually in the Milosevic trial at transcript page 12337 to 38, you talk about that relationship between Toso Pajic and Jovica Stanisic who was the head of the SDB in Serbia. Can you please elaborate a little bit. How do you know that Mr. Pajic was working for Mr. Stanisic as part of the SDB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My understanding that it was a very close relationship because I was present on several occasions in Mr. Pajic' office when Mr. Pajic made the right calls to Mr. Stanisic informing him of certain things that were happening on the day. So there was a constant traffic of information, if you like, between Mr. Pajic and Mr. Stanisic at the time. And when I eventually ended up back in Serbia, Mr. Pajic was installed in the office of SDB Serbia already which lead me to understand that he was working for them much earlier than it was presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say when we got back to Serbia, are you talking about after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Pajic, after Operation Storm, went to work for Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Or the SDB Serbia, yes. I'll make this clear. He worked for Mr. Stanisic before, but it was made official after we returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness pause between questions and answers for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning your attention to page 10 of your statement. This is the subject of the obstruction of the work of the ECMM. Now, you say in the statement: "Our sole objective was to obstruct the work of the ECMM, and later, of the UN. We did everything to keep them from finding out the truth, and we repeatedly supplied them with misinformation. It was amazing to us how often they believed what we were saying. But if you keep repeating the same lies again and again, it seems as if anyone would eventually conclude that it must be true, that no one could lie so often and so consistently." Can you give us an example of what type of misinformation, for example, you might provide to the ECMM or the UN as part of your job.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The first one that comes to mind would be how the Croatian nationals are living peacefully within the RSK; specifically in Sector North. We kept one village intact. It was a Croatian village, not too far from Topusko, maybe three or four kilometres away. And we have spent considerable time making sure that nothing happens to those guys, for PR reasons, obviously, not because we liked them extremely or -- yeah. It was just a matter of if any international -- member of international community would come in then we show this village and say, See. These guys are living here; they don't mind. Nothing is happening to them. That would be one of the instances. The other instances would be if the ECMM because they would -- at the time -- I need to explain this. At the time the members of the ECMM were not allowed to stay overnight in RSK at the beginning. They would return to Zagreb in the evening and then come back the following morning. And usually the night before, they would leave, they would give us the plans for the next day. For example, visiting a certain area which gave us all night to decide whether it is okay for them to see this or not. If the decision was, no, we shouldn't take them there, then we would come up with a reason why we can't take them the next morning. And that would be very easy to organise because we just create an incident between the forces of RSK and forces of Croatia that same night. And the military observers would be our witness if something did happen the previous night, and since of the sensitivity of the area, we cannot take them there. That would be one of the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would part of your job or part of this misinformation include trying to conceal locations of your heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely. I mean, you had to consider that the roads which the members of the ECMM motorcade would be taken through were already fairly far away from the actual positions of the ARSK artillery. And we had to make sure they stray away from the convoy itself, so it was always escorted by the police and military police at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now on the same page, page 10, you say that "every interpreter working with the UN and ECMM in the Krajina was reporting back to the SDB and was on our payroll." My question to you is: How is it that the RSK was able to control who the interpreters would be for the UN and the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was matter of employment. It was very obvious that the foreign nationals would need locals to work, whether it was a dishwasher or cleaners or interpreters or whatever happens. We just applied a very simple rule which is acceptable to the west, they would never question it, and that's that we need to have a background check of every potential employee of the UN, being a local. The UN themselves were not very willing, but they accepted it as such. So we would get, for example, the list of people who were applying for the jobs, and then we talk to them first. First we would appeal to their patriotism, if you like, that is their duty to any information they come across they should supply to us. And I carried of those meetings and instructions and make absolutely sure that they don't make decision what's important, what is not important. Every information they would get across should be given to us; we will analyse it and decide whether it was important or not. But I never believed the unimportant informations, every information had its own weight and importance. So once we organised that part, it was easy selling from there on because every employee was actually reporting to us. We were mostly concerned with interpreters because I physically could not be present at every meeting we had in my AOR, which is 70 kilometres long and about 20 kilometres wide. And there was always a meeting going on somewhere, whether it's a Red Cross, or ECMM, or military personnel of the UN, and they would use their own interpreters. But I made it absolutely clear that the minutes of the meeting and whatever resolutions had been made, end up on my desk the very same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to interpreters and local staff that didn't want to provide information to Serbian intelligence, what methods would you use to try to coerce them to working with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, honestly, I have to say it was unheard of that somebody would refuse to work with the government -- not government, the military, or whether the SDB or the KOS. But there were cases. There were the cases where they say, oh, no don't lead me into it. I just don't want to do it. They would pressurised, and if they still refused, they would not get a job, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How could you ensure that they wouldn't get a job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think the easiest way was to have them mobilised. If you have enough free time to go and work for the UN, you have free time to be on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you now trial Exhibit D701.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I showed this to you yesterday during our proofing. This is a 1993 document about one RSK intelligence operation called Horizont. Now, is the -- are the types of activities here, in terms of background checks on the interpreters, drivers, liaison officers, et cetera, attempts to liaise with UN members who demonstrate a certain bias towards us, et cetera, was that part of your overall understanding of what types of activity, Serbian intelligence was engaging in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I also mentioned that I never heard of action Horizont. So I never seen the document before, but what it does describe -- it describe what is I was doing, in my sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could Exhibit D702, please. If we could go to page 3 in the English. Towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I showed this to you yesterday. These are some operative actions directed against international organisations. If we look at the bottom, Operative Action Geneva directed against the EU Regional Centre in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is up in the 21st Corps Operative Action Rim, or Operative Action Rome, again monitoring the activities of the UNPROFOR members and international organisations in Sector South with headquarters in Topusko. Now, these types of operative actions, was this consistent with what types of activities you were doing, as part of your job in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that there may be a mistake in the translation when it says "in Sector South with headquarters in Topusko," if we could just check the original, because obviously Topuska is in Sector North; it's a little strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll check that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might interject. The original actually says Sector North.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we see that. But, at the same time, it is ... it's not just Sector South, but south between --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: North is in quotation marks, as well, in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now can you tell us the reporting chain when you would get information from interpreters or local staff, you would prepare a report and send that report where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the day let us assume there were seven meetings spread across the Sector North and I would get those reports. I will compile those reports, draw out which I consider to be of significant importance to us and write another report based on the reports which I have received, and I would hand them to Colonel Zimonja. Colonel Zimonja would read them and make a final decision who else get them. Whether the police would get them through Toso Pajic, and if some military concerns, then Cedo Bulat, the commanding officer of the 21st Corps, would get as copy as well. Or if he says, Nobody gets nothing, that was the end of the story for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go back to D701 for just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the second sentence of this operative action says: "The action shall be conducted in the entire territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina. Was it your understanding that the types of activities that you were engaged in were the types of intelligence activities that were being conducted throughout the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My belief was, yes, it was exactly the same in every sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to intelligence or information gathering before Operation Storm. Before I get to that was a copy of your report -- reports that you would gather from the field, would that also go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reports that you would prepare on the basis of information that you were getting from local staff, would a copy of those reports go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Automatically because Colonel Zimonja was there. So he would report it to his own [indiscernible]. But, again, we have to distinguish what we considered to be information of vital importance for Belgrade to know or what was of a local character that really doesn't have to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now turning to the issue of Operation Storm, in the Milosevic case, you testified at trial transcript page 12452 that an ECMM monitor named Bent Jensen informed you prior to Operation Storm of the time, strength of the attack, and direction of the attack that the Croatian army was planning. Can you tell us the circumstances around which Mr. Jensen approached you. Where did it happen, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We provided Mr. Jensen with a house which is only about a 100 yards away from my own house. So it was very easy for him to just walk down without being seen that he's coming to me, and vise versa, I could go to him. I didn't have to hide, but sometimes we felt maybe it's not a very good idea somebody else seen him coming to my home. On that particular evening he walked in, and he was rather shaky, and he said he has got some extremely informations for me. And then he by word of the month he told me about the time of the attack, which proves to be correct, the strength of the attack, direction of the attack. I've wrote it all down. He didn't give any documents, he just verbally informed me about it, but I did write it down. And then I [indiscernible] myself, took my caravan straight to the HQ, and submitted this report to the HQ of 21st Corps. I had a commanding officer which was not up to his task, really, so I took it upon myself to send a telex to Knin HQ. This is the last what I heard from them because the following morning the attack did start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D923 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is General Mrksic's report after Operation Storm from the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 of 29 on the English. Mr. Registrar, it's the first sentence under section 2 which would be page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in his report of the 26th of August, General Mrksic reports: "At 1400 hours on 3 August 1995, the Main Staff learned that the aggression would commence at 0500 hours on 4 August. All the commanders and unit commanders were informed about the aggression's commencement time." Does this time, 1400 hours on 3 August, is that possibly around the time-period that you sent your telex from Sector North down to Knin HQ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an organigram that you used with the Prosecution in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is going to be 65 ter 1D2685, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic, this is an organigram, I believe, which you put together; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this organigram attempts to portray the relationships between RSK politicians, the SDB of Serbia, the Yugoslav army, and the ARSK. And if you could just in your own words try to explain what the relationships are between all these entities.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the screen here, then I -- on the left-hand side you have the RSK politician, below is RSK MUP, and above is SDB of Serbia. And you see the names of the people that I actually dealt myself personally with. So you will see that they are all interconnected. Below you see the Arkan's forces. Now both of these -- there is a line going directly to the SDB of the Serbia. Colonel Lolenik [phoen] and Colonel Bozovic, in the top square just below Frenki Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic, are the commanding officers of the special units of police of Serbia, which were deployed in Bosnia in Pauk command, which you could see in centre of the square, Pauk HQ Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's stop right there for one moment. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what was the Pauk HQ Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Pauk HQ Bosnia was the HQ which combined the forces of Fikret Abdic of the western Bosnia, together with the special units of the Serbian police on the ground, the members of the 21st Corps on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 21st Corps of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: RSK, okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a joint operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now if you could continue -- let me ask you some questions first. What is the relationship between the SDB of Serbia and the RSK MUP, in your organigram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you had the representative of -- let's use the source word [B/C/S spoken], DB, on which head is Milos Pajic, who is officer of the RSK police. And you have Toso Pajic who later on became a minister of interiors. Now both of these people were in direct connection or direct line of communication with Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade. Or let us assume Jovica Stanisic was visiting his troops in RSK, he would make a conduct with these two people as well, on the ground. So directly connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at the box that says "SDB Serbia." Underneath them you have Arkan and his forces. But within the box you have Frenki Simatovic and then Colonel Ulemek Legija, and then Colonel Bozovic or --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bozovic. Can you explain what the forces are commanded by Simatovic, Legija, and Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The forces under their commands are the members of the special police of the DB of Serbia, which were deployed in Pauk and RSK at the time. The commanding officers were Colonel Bozovic and Colonel Unik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic headed HQ in Petrova Gora, which is within the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The other two guys, they were on the other side in Bosnia with their HQ, where they are directly responsible to Frenki Simatovic in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now page -- while we still have this on the screen, at page 13 of your statement, you say in the third full paragraph: "Surla and Karan sent all my reports to Zimonja in Belgrade and the tapes that I made of meetings were forwarded to a subordinate of Stanisic who I only knew as Medo."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually I handed those tapes personally to a person who introduced himself to me as a Medo, and that was within the building of the SDB in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Specific tape, something to do with the German ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in Medo.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is only time I met this gentleman. I'm not aware of his real name. He was introduced to me as Medo; hey, I'm Medo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of an individual named Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I did hear of him, but I never saw him. Never saw him. Never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a unit known as the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only what was available through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know that Slobodan Medic was commander of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I did find out that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As someone familiar with nicknames, Medic Medo, and I understand this is just trying to help us out, you don't know for as a fact, but could someone named Medic have a nickname like Medo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Quite possible. Any large person, his physical, huge in appearance might as well called Medo. Medo is a kind of diminutive for a bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have Exhibit D948, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to take you some telephone intercepts during Operation Storm, Mr. Lazarevic, and see if you can help us decipher who is on the phone based on your knowledge that you have expressed in your witness statement and in your testimony today. These are conversations from the Knin HQ on the evening of the 4th of August. Now this is a conversation between Medo and Zezelj, and then later on with General Mrksic in Knin. And if you look -- in the first part of the conversation is this short conversation between Medo, identified and the end in the transcript and Zezelj whose with the Z in the diacritic. And then at a few lines down, approximately ten, G, who is General Mrksic appears on the line. And he says, Hello, Medo. And It says, You alive, and goes on. A few lines down, Mrksic says to Medo: "The rest, considering the battles is fine, there was a little bit something up there in Velebit. Your guys did it well. There is one of your guys wounded up there? Now, it seems that Medo is someone who has men under his command based on this conversation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apparently reading from this, yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge of Operation Storm, this battle near the Velebit that's taking place between the RSK and forces under -- under the HV special police. Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't really know. I would like to point out something to the learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the time that all this is happening, I had my hands full of happenings in the Sector North. Not all the reports from the other sectors would come to my desk at this particular time; I'm talking August 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th. So this what I'm looking at now, I can only take it at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And by analysing it, yes, I would say are you probably correct, but I would not state my reputation on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of all these different units, is it possible that Medo here is a reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has clearly stated his lack of knowledge on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic had not yet finished his question, as a matter of fact. But, Mr. Lazarevic, Could you please wait before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not -- it's not a reason for apology. But Mr. Hedaraly objected to a question which had not been yet been fully phrased yet. So Mr. Misetic now formulates his question, you not answer it, and then we'll first rule on the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will ask a few more questions and then get back to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you at this moment withdraw that question, and -- yes, well, that matter has then been resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go down a few lines on the same page, General Mrksic says -- again, this is 2158 hours on the 4th of August: "Well, we will defend Knin tomorrow and the day after tomorrow in any way we can." And if we can turn the page, please. He says: "Knin is empty, but we will defend." Medo says: "Okay, your friends are here at my place, and they want to say hello." PS, a friend X and Mrksic participate in the further course of the conversation. So Medo hands the phone to someone who is identified as X, and I will ask you some questions. Maybe you can help us out with this. But there's long conversation then about the strategy to employ in defending Knin. X in the middle of the page says: "Don't wait for him down there but above Knin. Don't wait for him down there, Mrksa. Mind that you keep Gracac." And then it goes on. If we turn the page, see who X might be. On page 3, towards the bottom, please. Third line from the bottom. Now the transcript records it as General Mrksic saying: "Okay, okay, Feki, we are hanging in." Based on your knowledge of Mr. Simatovic, could that in fact be, Okay, okay, Frenki, we are hanging in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there's a few things now. First of all, he is leading the witness through this. If he wants the witness to read the document and then see if he can identify the people, that's one thing. To give his own interpretation of what it says and then ask the witness. Secondly, the witness has stated that he has no knowledge of this conversation, anything that happened in that area on that day, so to that extent, it calls for speculation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily. But the question was not a bit leading but was -- you more or less whispered a possible answer in the ear of the witness which is not what you're supposed to do, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll tie that up with the next conversation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He goes on, Hey, Mrksa, we are packing the items for you down there this evening." Then next line says: "Why didn't you do that two days ago?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first line X says: "Well, ask the one whom you had a meeting with." And then there's a line in the middle: "Okay, then, Feki, see you." Now that's at 2158, and let's go to the conversation that takes place ten minutes later, which is 1D2706, please. Now first to address Mr. Hedaraly's objection, if we could go to the bottom of the first page in the English. Now this -- in this conversation which is 12 minutes later, Mrksic says: "I spoke to Frenki." Now how many Frenkis did you know in your entire life, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Had you ever heard of any other person named Frenki in any political or military circles in Serbia, Bosnia, or the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of Serbian origin, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this conversation is -- at the top, purports to be a conversation between Milan Martic and Mile Mrksic with a certain Jole from SRY. Now they refer to him as Jole throughout the conversation except -- if we could turn the page, please. Scroll down to the bottom. Above the 73, no sound. One, two, the third-speaking person there. M-r-k. They call him Jole through the conversation, and then towards the end Mrksic says: "Jovica, don't bother." Now based on what you testified in your statement your knowledge of the structures of the RSK, the relationships, how many Jovicas did you know that were in positions of authority in Serbia, Bosnia, or the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the conversation between Martic, Mrksic, and a certain Jole. And if -- there's a beginning part of that conversation, I'm interested in the bottom. Mrksic says: "I spoke to Frenki, Meda. They are coming; they are leaving tomorrow. It is 200 people, but the important thing is to defend Knin tomorrow." If we turn the page, please. "Hang in there tomorrow. I'll be there the day after tomorrow." And then towards the bottom above the line that says: "Jovica don't bother," Jole says: "I will gather around who I have here, and I'll be on my way there." Now, based on what you've testified so far about the only person you know named Frenki would be Frenki Simatovic, and the only person in authority that you know named Jovica is Jovica Stanisic. They talk about 200 people coming. Who would they have at their disposal based on your knowledge that would amount to 200 people coming to the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That would be the 200 people which were deployed in RSK in the HQ of Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And those 200 people, based on your knowledge, who were they under the direct command of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Direct command, Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is this now -- in the organigram you said there were two units under the SDB's control, one which -- one line which led to Arkan, the other line which led to Milorad Ulemek Legija. Which of those two would this refer to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Ulemek units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Legija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D2076 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's all of the transcripts on the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two pages. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that is an extract from a larger 65 ter number, so there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it used to be 65 ter 2814, which is 150 pages excerpt that we've taken these two out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other Defence counsel no objection either. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1463 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk a little bit about your presence at peace negotiations, and if we could have Exhibit D922 on the screen, please. Now, this is at least one -- I don't want to call it, protocol of the members of both parties that attended the delegation, indicating your presence as an interpreter of the Serb delegation and Kosta Novakovic being the head of the delegation. Now can you explain why -- what your role was there attending these conferences? It says officially your role is as an interpreter. I believe you have clarified that in your statement, but perhaps you can explain it a bit further.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, this meeting, the limit of the numbers of the delegates was very limited. To make me a part of the delegation and yet to fulfill my role as a representative of KOS during the meeting, I was named interpreter. So I became the part of official delegation itself. But if I look at it, all these four people here on the Serbian delegation, they're all KOS members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How do you know Kosta Novakovic is a KOS member?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zimonja told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You have to realize, I mean, none of the these people carries any specific badge on their uniforms to identify them as being KOS or DB or whatever. So you rely on information given to you by your superior. And I had no reason to doubt Colonel Zimonja if he told that Colonel Novakovic is a KOS, so, Don't worry about him; he is one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when Colonel Zimonja told you this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When this list was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, you jumped ahead of me a little bit, but let me show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D2074 on the screen, please. If we could go to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First of all, while this is on the screen, that is a picture of you, obviously, and who is the person in camouflage there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the fifth picture, please. Now, can you tell us, who is in this picture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is me there, with the red beret on the head and next to me is Colonel Kosta Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with Kosta Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Over a period of five years, maybe half a dozen times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who else was present when Colonel Zimonja told you that Mr. Novakovic was a member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nobody. Just me and Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender these pictures into evidence at this time. And there are, I think, three others that we will -- sorry. There are six in total we will come back to the four during the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you already want the whole series.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From practical purposes [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We can have them MFI now, and then when they go through it, we can have them tender them formally when the witness confirms that they are his pictures. It seems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whole series to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the pictures have been authenticated in the statement, so -- and they were produced to us by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are -- you would say yes, although he is asked about who appears, although the photographs are not identified as such in the statement itself. I think, at least at the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They are, Mr. President. Because they are numbered, and the numbers correspond to the numbers in the statements, and the numbers, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then still the numbers ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will get back to this and make sure that they are numbered in a way that with tie them to the specific number that he has used in the witness statement. We are only tendering six out of the 90 pictures that he references in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These six selected pictures will receive a number, but they will be MFIed until we have dealt with all of them and that a decision on admission will be taken. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why don't I go through them right now. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, if we could take a look at picture 2, please. Can you tell us where this picture was taken.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During one of the meetings in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And was this while you were a member of a Serb delegation attending a peace conference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who some of the people are in the picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could blow it up a little bit please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There's me on the left. Next to me Emir Rakic [phoen] who was the minister of defence of RSK at the time. Next to him, third from the left, is the guy to do something with security. The lady in the middle was a private secretary of president - then - Goran Hadzic, who is the guy with the beard. Gentleman behind Hadzic, again something to do with security, personal security of President Hadzic. And I have no recollection of the gentleman on the last position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next picture, please. Now do you recall who these individuals are?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember them anymore by the name. But we found this to be a rather laughing matter in my own HQ because it's so easy to actually map the positions of the UNPROFOR. Just pretending to be nice to the guys and let's have a shot together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A shot of what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, three of us, but basically I wanted the map behind it, not them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could explain this a little bit --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is taken notice UN HQ. This is their operational room. The map which they have on the wall would have all the markings where the units are placed on both sides of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We wanted that picture. And I know these guys wanted their photo taken with me. So I suggested -- this is a nice place, you know, we got a map behind us, you know, and so you can see on the faces they are thrilled. And these guys are colonels, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again now these -- the people in white, where are they from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is taken during the presidency of the EC by the Greeks. And these guys, both Greeks, representatives of the Greek government within the ECMM. And this is a kind of, I don't know, a picnic day between us and Greeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe the next one we have seen, so if we could go to picture 6, please. Do you recall what picture this is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Some kind of a banquet somewhere in RSK in the northern sector, like, I don't know. Every month some of the battalions would have a special day, is a day of the republic, and they have this, and they have that, and they would invite officers from the RSK. Now I was always the one to attend those. So right here you see -- oh, yeah, I remember. Now I remember because I see the both guys. The guy sitting next to me on my left is outgoing commanding officer of the Jordanian battalion. And next to him is the incoming commanding officer of the Jordanian battalion. And the colonel; he's a polish colonel; he was a sector commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I believe that is complete, and we tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Series of six photograph, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from other Defence teams. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At page 14 of your statement you say that the delegations and now we have seen that you were in Geneva as well as two others that you reference in your statement. At page 14 you discuss having -- that the delegation had to travel to Belgrade to be briefed in Belgrade prior to going to these international peace conferences. Can you tell us a little bit about what you were told during your briefings in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First we -- you have to know something, that these delegations were split in two separate bodies. Are we under attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it your job to know? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military part of delegation and a political side of delegation. Now the military part is always the one that I was a part of. We would meet with the Croatian military and discuss purely military things. Either a -- DMZ zones or how far we should pull the artillery back, how close should the units be close the border itself, and things like that. And we always managed to get to agreement very, very quickly because he are military guys; they have very brief and concise, and they know what they are doing. The political side of the delegation is one had to be instructed over and over again, what they can agree and what they cannot not agree on. And it was maybe even simpler for them to understand if they were told, Do not agree on anything. So basically our preparations for the meeting, whether it is in Geneva or Norway or wherever it happens to be, was to repeat those instructions again, stressing the position that we cannot agree. And if we are cornered during the meeting that we actually had to give an answer yes or no, and yet not ready to give our open no to it, we will almost have a little stipulation there. Yes, basically we agreed to it, but it has to be submitted to the people's assembly to make a final decision on it, meaning we have to go back to RSK, present it to the parliament, and if parliament decide it is okay, that our signatures given in Vienna, for example, are valid. But if the parliament decided no, it's no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You indicate at page 15 that two of these briefings were conducted by Jovica Stanisic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you come to form an understanding as to what was the purpose of -- of not agreeing to anything?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, none of the people who briefed us would actually tell us openly why we are not to agree. But analysing the situation before, after, during, it was very simple to figure out what is the real reason. The real reason is to keep tension high in RSK and take the tension away, or rather focus on things which were happening in Belgrade at the time. And that is the time when Milosevic was fortifying his position, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did there ever come a time when -- that you were aware that the position of Belgrade with respect to these peace negotiations had changed in any material way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not really. For all I knew, was pointless to go back and listen to the same thing over again. Because I know the instructions is going to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Don't agree on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But sometimes the Croatian side made it easy not to agree. For example, when they asked us to pull out artillery pieces 25 kilometres from [indiscernible] Kupa river, they would place us in the vicinity of Bihac, which is like another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that it's 10.30, and this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is time for a break. And perhaps in order to avoid anyone at any later stage reading our transcripts, will be fully flabbergasted by what was said, when the witness said, Are we under attack, this was in response to some loud bangs which could be heard in the courtroom, and that's what made him -- triggered him to say this. And after my response, there was at least some laughter in the courtroom. We will have a break and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, two very small procedural matters. The Chamber has received a copy of the agreement on confidentiality of 65 ter material. We are looking into the matter, but most likely the parties will be invited to -- to file the agreement so that it's on the record. But before doing this, we'd like to look at it a second time. The other issue is, witness AG61. The Chamber has received some information, I take it, Mr. Misetic, that you have received it as well. And the suggestion would be that it might be good to get relevant documents in cooperation with VWS, so as to have a more solid basis for whatever decision is to be taken on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Mr. President. I think when I spoke to the witness, the issue was coming here versus videolink because of the health issue and not -- not testifying at all. Yes. So I would agree that if VW could assist us in determining the status of the health --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that you will be then be in touch with VWS because it was said that there would be documents, and let's now have a look at it and see what these documents tell us and what the consequence would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will look into that. Mr. President, my understanding of the e-mail was that the witness said he cannot afford health care, and therefore it may be an issue of financing a medical exam which I don't know what the procedure is, but we will deal with VWU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, waiting-lists well-known in the territory we are on at this moment as far as medical care is concerned, but financing, of course, is another problem. Let's try to find out what actually the situation. Finally the Chamber was informed about some -- an issue about broadcasting the court proceedings. The Chamber is not in a position to give it any follow-up at this moment but the Chamber is informed about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, picking up where we left off last, I'd like to turn your attention to the Pauk command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could first have D923 on the screen again, please. If we could have page 2, please, in the English. The middle paragraph. Actually, I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. Could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there are two issues that I'm going to cover with you on the basis of these two pages, so let's just cover them both right now. This is again General Mrksic's report of 26 August 1995. And at the bottom of the first page, General Mrksic reports: "In June there was a day and night work on reorganizing the existing military organisation and establishing new units out of military conscripts who were being brought from the territory of the SRY. At the so-called saint Vitus day parade, there were exhibited the potential possibilities of the new military organisation." And a bit later on I will show you a video from that parade. So it's to ask you to identify people on the video. "Strengthening of the" - if we could turn the page please - "established organisation and making it capable of carrying out combat activities required a minimum time-period of 2 to 3 months (the reorganisation of the SVK, which had already started, was planned to conclude until the beginning of October, at the latest)." And if we skip a paragraph and go to the next paragraph. "The operation Mac, or Sword 95, on the territory of western Bosnia started on 19 July 1995 and could have been carried out successfully only if our units had been prepared to carry out, at the same time, an attack operation of the operative level in the area of western Bosnia and a defence operation of a strategic character with the borders Republic of Croatia." "After ten days, the Operation Sword was stopped because of the attack on Grahovo and the endangerment of Knin from the direction of the Dinara mountains. The moves carried out were those the SVK was forced to make in order to stabilize the front towards Knin after the fall of Grahovo." And I would like you to -- to go into you into some details that in your statement because the Operation Mac is some background about what took place in Operation Strom. And going back to the Pauk command -- sorry, if we could turn to the page and let me show you something that General Mrksic said in this report. "The initiation of the operations against the 5th Muslim Corps" -- which is the corps in Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Without the necessary readiness particularly damaged the SVK which was always, as if according to some rule, being pushed into fighting for the territories of western Bosnia." And we'll get to this issue of the SVK being pushed into fighting for the territories of western Bosnia in a minute. But going back to this issue of the SVK's operations on the Bihac pocket. You told us about the Pauk command. Do you recall an operation to take the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And it happened earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a combined operation of a 5 Corps, two from Bosnia and Bosnian Serbian republic, and from our own parts, from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Within the Pauk command was there any involvement of any other units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Pauk consisted of the units from the western Bosnian troops belonging to Fikret Abdic. The special units of police from Serbia proper and the Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the Milosevic case at trial transcript page 12321, you said the operations would require consultation with Belgrade. Now, why would operations require consultation with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The magnitude of the attack could not be organised on a corps level. It has to be organised by the general HQ in Belgrade because it involved the troops from the Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if it also involved as you just said the troops of the -- I'm sorry, the units of Serbia proper, would it -- you distinguish -- let me rephrase the question. The troops of Serbia proper that you have indicated were operating in the Pauk command, who do they belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say RSK and the VRS, do you mean --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking a military part of it. The police itself, it's entirely different thing. They would get their instructions from Stanisic anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this operation required consultation with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From discussion taken in the operation room of my own corps, within the commanding officers, the visiting officers from Pauk, telephone conversations with the Belgrade HQ of the police and the -- and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge being in the HQ, let me show you something else, which is, Mr. Registrar, 1D2674. This has been provided to the Defence by the Office of the Prosecutor, and these are the likely handwritten notes of Ratko Mladic covering 27 January 1995 through 5 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And we would like to go to English page 201; and B/C/S page 206, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before we continue, you just referred to the Milosevic transcript, to a page which at least is not one of the printed out pages for me as being the selection. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mistake by me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if it is, of course, part of the transcript, then referring to it is referring to what is in evidence. If not, then, of course, it could be considered to be leading, and Mr. Hedaraly did not complain. But I would like to -- I didn't have this one on -- it starts at 12336, but it could be that I've got the wrong portion printed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was not part of it. I -- I did note it. I did not object because it didn't seem to be a critical matter, but it is not what was in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I always like to know whether we are referring to something which is in evidence or something which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will move later to add that page then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily if Mr. Hedaraly does not -- if that is reflected in that page, If you out it to the witness. It's just a kind of a general reminder that if reference is made that it's always clear whether it's reference to something which is or something which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are Mr. Mladic's notes - if I could get the - it says Belgrade, 29 June 1995. You can see on the first page, it's a meeting between President Milosevic, Bulatovic, Perisic, and Mrksic. And SM, likely Slobodan Milosevic. "Now have you stopped the Croatian Muslim offensive, we helped you, but we are at our last gasp. Republika Srpska is ensured, we must seal it and place emphasis on the RSK and defend it."
