If we could turn the page, please, two pages to the third page, page 203, please. There's a discussion: "We must install Republika Srpska and then defend Republika Srpska Krajina. What would you give them, I ask him?" "Slobodan Milosevic: I would give them Vogosca, and Ilijas. They need a link with Sarajevo, Zenica, and Tuzla. We would enlarge on account of Fikret, I would not touch the enclaves, they are islands which will run out?" Now, there a reference to Fikret there. Based on your experience, who might Fikret be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at this, "we would large on account of Fikret," what would you interpret that to mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It looks to me like he was swapping territories really. On the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Excuse me. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that there needs to be a proper foundation laid before about what happened. And if the witness has any knowledge of that, rather than ask him to interpret something that is said on that date. If he knows anything about these event, if he knows anything about such a meeting before jumping straight to reading a portion and asking him to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, perhaps the most -- the right way would be to ask whether he has any factual knowledge of the matter, and if not, this would not -- and at least I did not understand your objection to be, Mr. Hedaraly, that with the knowledge of the witness of the context of events that he might not have a clue of understanding on what it says. But the first question, I tend to agree with, Mr. Hedaraly, should be, do you have any factual knowledge of this conversation or direct knowledge and on the second then to start interpreting what it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, were you present in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this meeting specifically?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that you lived in the Bihac area for many years and participated or had knowledge of the attacks on the Bihac pocket, do you think you could assist in understanding who Fikret might be and the circumstances of this attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have always been willing to -- to assist the Court in their findings, but these things, you will require of me to read something which I'm not familiar with and then to make an assessment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask about your knowledge, then, of what transpired on the ground on the basis of -- and ask you whether it was consistent with what is actually in these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to numbered page 206, please, and it's B/C/S page 211.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is meeting the 30th of June, 1995, with President Milosevic and -- at the Yugoslav army General Staff. Were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The first line is: "I called Fikret Abdic to tell us what is new in the Bihac pocket, that is a very important point for us, we must do something so can he can take Cazin, and then it will be easier later." Now, subsequently, do you know whether the -- part of the ARSK operations involving the VRS and the Serbian police unit -- was Cazin part of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would be at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to interject again. But I don't know at which point now when this becomes leading, when the witness says he doesn't know anything about it, to read him a portion of it and then say, Is that -- do you know what happened after? Do you know what happened before? Mr. Misetic should first explore what is his knowledge about the events and then show him the document. Otherwise, it's a -- akin to leading the within on something he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, of course, showing a witness something which he hasn't seen before about a meeting which he has not attended, finally leads to some kind of leading under all circumstances. I think, Mr. Hedaraly, you're inviting Mr. Misetic to take it step by step and to going from non-leading to, perhaps, the level of leading where you might start objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I just think that that's also what would assist the Chamber the best in finding out this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tried to call the author of the notebook, but he wouldn't take my call. Mr. Mladic was unavailable. Mr. Milosevic, is, as you know, unavailable. So to that extent, this notebook is without foundation until Mr. Hedaraly contacts Mr. Mladic and secures his arrival here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let me stop you here. Of course, the foundation Mr. Hedaraly is seeking is not perhaps, finally he would, but is not to invite you at this moment to all the author. That seems to not be the issue he is raising. I think you perfectly understood the issue he is raising is to take it step by step. First of all, were you present at the meeting? Have you any knowledge about what apparently is referred to this in meeting? And then only at -- when you have checked that all, only then it could well be that the witness has some knowledge about the events described here, and then first to explore what he knows about it, and if he has no knowledge of that, whether, in reading it, in its context, it rings a bell to anything he has knowledge of, either contextual knowledge or direct knowledge. I think that's what Mr. Hedaraly is seeking, and not blaming you at this moment for not having Mr. Mladic here as a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you know if units of under Jovica Stanisic's command participated in the attacks on the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the police forces participated in the -- in the Pauk command --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of the attack on Bihac. I know both of these that you mentioned were involved there attacks in Cazin section of western Bosnia, around Kladusa, not deep down to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, my mistake. When I say Bihac, I'm referring to the whole enclave, not just the city. So are you aware of the attacks -- of attacks by units under Jovica Stanisic's command on the Bihac enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of forces under General Mrksic's command engaging in attacks on the Bihac enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any idea what the objective of attacking the Bihac enclave was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The understanding was to ensure the passage of the railway between Belgrade and Knin via Banja Luka. There is a certain section of the pocket that the railway goes through. And to that extent, we needed that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I can do it on cross-examination, but if we can get the source of the witness's understanding, it may be more efficient to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How do you know that that was an objective of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a matter of discussion of the HQ, my own HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was in the HQ at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat, myself, Toso Pajic. It was a subject of discussion on a number of meetings that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could first finish this. Based on your answers now, let me take you to this conversation. I think you have already stated you don't have personal knowledge of a meeting in Belgrade on the 30th of June, 1995, involving Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Stanisic, and Fikret Abdic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this page, then, based on what you've just said in terms of the participation of the Serbian police units, it says: "Legija and Bozovic had contact with Nanic through a Motorola." Do you know who Bozovic is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Bozovic is a colonel of the special police unit from Belgrade. And he had his headquarters in Velika Kladusa itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "We can take Cazin in two weeks if we had 1500 men." And then it says: "JS, expansion unknown." I guess we'll deal with who JS might be later. "But which forces can General Mrksic engage?" And then there's discussion. If we turn the page, please. SM, Slobodan Milosevic, says: "I think it's important to resolve the 5th Corps," which again is the army of BiH in the Bihac --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Under the command of General Dudakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. "I think it is important to resolve the 5th Corps as soon as possible and then later to try cutting off near Livno." And then there's further discussions if we turn the page about subordinating the Pauk command to General Mrksic, et cetera. Based on your answers is this discussion about the different elements that are to participate in the attack on Bihac consistent with what actually took place on the ground in Bihac around the middle of July in terms of units of participating in the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you first I have very limited knowledge of what was going on over there. I had a sufficient trouble in my own area of operation to know exactly what is happening around Bihac pocket. It is consistent with the general idea of taking Bihac pocket once, and that's it. And we attempted it on several occasion in a previous four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Mladic diary is extensive, and we do intend to use it extensively during Defence case in chief or various portions of it, mostly starting from 1 June 1995 through, I think it ends September 5th 1995. I don't know how you wish to deal with it, whether we move it all it now or portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that there would be some -- relevance-wise, it may make more sense to do it portion by portion. IT can be added to the same exhibit number as they get tendered in court. But I think to have the whole diary in now wholesale without what the relevance is may be a little bit burdensome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there are three options, I think. The first is to take it part by part, which might create a risk that we lose sight of what we're talking about. The other way would be to have the whole of it marked for identification and then make later a selection on the basis of what we've looked at and what apparently are the portions which neither of the parties have given any attention to. And the other way would be to build up rather than to scale down. I think the portion by portion might not be the best idea. Perhaps we start with the whole of it marked for identification and then to finally make up our mind as what would be the relevant portions on the basis of what we've looked at, which would mean that we would have all the 334 pages e-court English and of course original marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I whole-heatedly agree, Mr. President, specifically for the benefit of our case managers in terms of up-loading and taking out documents that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I was thinking about them first. Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number to the Mladic diary which would then be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1465, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we have looked at this moment at -- in the English e-court version, the meeting the 30th of June was page 206 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S 206. I will read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have in English 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we did the following, which I believe English page 201, which is a meeting in Belgrade on the 29th of June, and that is also B/C/S page 206. We then used English page 203, which is B/C/S page 208. And then we used English pages 206 through 211, which is B/C/S pages 211 through 216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my understanding, looking at page 206 in English - I'll just get it on my screen - it starts with, "I called FA..." and then soon after that, FA is introduced as speaking, or not speaking. How -- what's the interpretation of the parties? Of course, I'm not yet analysed anything, but the meeting is between Yugoslav army General Staff and Milosevic which does not necessarily -- No, it's at the Yugoslav army General Staff. Oh, the -- yes, I see it now. But then it starts with: "I called to tell us," et cetera, and then it continues with FA, as if he were speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe he is speaking, Mr. President. I think he is saying. The way I interpreted it, Mr. Milosevic introduces the meeting by saying, in essence, I have called FA to come and tell us about what is new in the Bihac pocket and then turns the floor over to FA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's just for me to understand that he did not only call him to invite him, but he apparently followed that invitation then and was present. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how you interpret? I'm also looking at the Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was trying to consult with a native B/C/S speaker to see if there was any light that can be gained from the original. I think there is an ambiguity whether he is referring to a phone conversation that he had and that is what being reported, or whether "I called" to mean I called him to attend this meeting. I don't think from the face of this a page it is entirely clear which one it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although on page 209, for example, in English, FA is introduced as speaking again. The same on 210. So it -- just for us to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sure we can look at carefully, and I'm sure we can agree with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Misetic on how to interpret it once we take a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that would be appreciated, because I do understand that Mr. Lazarevic could not help us out on who was present during that meeting on the 30th of June. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, I believe, Mr. President, I have selected this portion from the Milosevic trial; transcript page 12343.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You testified that my experience has shown that we are not talking about three different armies - meaning Yugoslavia, Republika Srpska, and RSK - we are talking about one and only one army, and that's the JNA. Whether the name was VRS or RSK army was totally irrelevant in real terms because all the supplies and the finances would come from Yugoslavia. And I just wanted to ask you to explain that a little bit further. Why do you say that they were all one army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would it not be correct to finish the quote and say the supplies and the finances would come from Yugoslavia, Serbia, if you like?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on it's next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, back to me? For all the purposes we are talking one army. When the JNA originally withdrew from Croatia and went into Bosnia and all the way to proper Serbia all the officer corps were the JNA officers. And they remained -- they remained in their position how they were before. If Colonel Bulat was a corps commander, he was not a corps commander before the corps was formed and then he was made a corps commander of the Kordun Corps, the 21st Corps. But he was still a JNA. Those supplies that we get we would get through Bosanski Posavina, all the way to Knin. For example, a large convoy would start from Belgrade, and then as it comes to a certain destinations, it would leave behind, I don't know, 10 trucks, 15 trucks, and then and then continue. The rest of the convoy will come to us, and we keep another five trucks assigned to us and the convoy continue further down. So it was a -- it was obvious that the original convoy, for example, had 30 trucks in it. By the time it reached us, it was down to 15. The rest of was left behind in Bosnia under certain posts. A paymaster would come every month from Belgrade to distribute the salaries to the officers which were on the JNA payroll. So you had a paymaster from Knin supplying the finances from Knin to those appointed by Knin. And you have a paymaster from Belgrade coming to supply the salaries or the money for the salaries for the officers appointed by Belgrade HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Concerning -- let me ask you, do you have knowledge as to command or coordination of military activities between Belgrade, the VRS, and the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I do possess, one which is actually relevant to the Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And it is happening in Sector North, I would be informed about it. Everything else was just I heard it by chance or I attended a meeting that is discussing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this. You've already provided testimony that the Pauk command, for example, contained elements of police from Serbia proper, the ARSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in that relationship, who has the overall command of those units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Original operations, it would definitely be the police from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Anyone in particular that you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic would be the one who was in charge of that. And his HQ was within the AOR of the 21st Corps. The rest of the Pauk was in Bosnia already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the railway. And I'd like to show you a map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1D2705, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this map depicts the situation in July 1995 with the various front lines in the area and the international borders. Do you see the black line that leads from Knin and snakes to Banja Luka. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's existing railway from the days of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And this rail -- we stopped it at Banja Luka. Do you know if that existing rail goes anywhere east of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware any train traffic going through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But in the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it was quite frequent. It was used regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was that railway go east of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It goes down to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. If you look at Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does it go east anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It begins and finishes in Banja Luka. Goes all the way to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. Is this the train that was one of the aims of -- this railway line, was this one of the aims of the attack on the Bihac enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was led to believe that is the main purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this, as I just tell you that we didn't draw to Belgrade because it would have required to us zoom out further which would have made the picture in Bihac enclave very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can get some clarification from the witness. Initially, when he was asked whether there was a rail going anywhere east, he said in 1995, he said no. Then later he said yes. Just see if we can clarify that because we have now two conflicting answers. We don't have any objection to the exhibit, but if we can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could also then clarify whether it begins and finishes in Banja Luka, which was unclear as an answer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I think it was unclear, when you were talking about the fact that the line was not operational in 1995, which portions of the line were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason for that being?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Ongoing conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this line from Banja Luka east, and I'm sorry, obviously you know that east of Banja Luka is Serbia. So from Banja Luka east was the line that you testified that line goes to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that line, that portion of the line, Belgrade-Banja Luka was operational in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you know why?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea; I can only assume because of the things that were happening in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. President, we tender the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you're invited to look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was going see if we could have the witness repeat the answer because it didn't appear on the transcript, at least in this draft stage, at line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that line, the portion of the line from Belgrade to Banja Luka was operational in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty certain it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. From the other Defence team, I expect an active position if there are any objections, so in situation of silence, I'll assume that there are no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1466.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've discussed the St. Vitus Day, or the Vidovdan, parade on June 28, 1995, which was referenced in Mr. Mrksic's report of 26th of August. And can you tell us, first of all, in your own words what is was the purpose of that parade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Showing off the strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The strength of what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: RSK army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And why, if you know, was the RSK army trying to show of its strength?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Lifting up the morale of the personnel on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you were asked in the -- by the Prosecution in the Milosevic trial, you were shown a video and asked to identify people on that video. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to do the same thing with you for just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this video is 1D2677. We are not using any audio here; we're just interested in the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify any of the people in this picture. And this is it -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Person in the middle, that's Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be Milorad Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ulemek, Legija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, this is at 9 seconds in the video. Do you recognise either of the gentlemen on the left or the right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking in this screen, in the bottom right-hand corner, there's a gentleman wearing a hat - I'm not talking about the man in the green beret, but the man next to him in the row behind him wearing a hat. Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The old Serbian army hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Second row, last on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That gentleman where the arrow is now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't make him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right there. Is that any better for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is better, but I don't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The gentleman in the front row there with the red beret. Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And obviously the man speaking is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mile Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan. He wasn't called for this specific occasion from Belgrade. He was in Krajina for about four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who Captain Dragan was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First have you to learn something about the Serbian mentality. We need heros, always did, and to my knowledge, always developed this cartoon character heroes. Captain Dragan is one of them. Apparently what I heard about him -- not a great deal, really, that he was operating some training camps down around Knin; that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That he was operating some installation in Belgrade to do with helping the injured soldiers or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender the video into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's first put on the record that when you asked who this was that we were at 40 seconds into the video, where we see a man with a Red Beret saluting. Mr. Hedaraly, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, no. But at page 62, line 1, I think if we can correct that the witness -- I think the -- perhaps the witness should repeat what he had said about who Captain was and whether he was called or not from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, our transcript is not complete. Could you when you were asked whether you knew who it was, I think you said Captain Dragan, he wasn't called for Belgrade for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was called from Belgrade for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. If you try to speak a bit more slowly, then that might save time in -- at a later stage. No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'm going to turn to page 20 of your 1999 statement, which is D1461. And this is where you talk about the existence of a standing policy of the RSK to force Croats from the Krajina and that each corps within the RSK army was expected to have units available to do dirty jobs towards this end. "It was tasked with targeting Croat civilians and creating a climate of fear." Now how do you know of the existence of these units available to do dirty jobs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I met him single, every day. And they had their own little HQ on the road between Vrginmost and Vojnic. And some of those guys, as I said, I met every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In that same page you described -- you say: "The existence of the RSK was dependant on the Serb population believing that they could never live with the Croats and anyone who challenged this proposition, such as Obradovic, was seen as a threat to the RSK government." My first question is if can you explain why the existence of the RSK was dependant on the Serb population believing that they could never live with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The general idea is to create a Serbian state within Croatia. That was the idea. Whether they call it a Greater Serbia or they call it this and that, but the idea was to form a Serbian or pure Serbia state within Croatian borders, and that was the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But why -- why do you relate the creation of a pure Serbian state within Croatia with the need to make the Serb population believe that they could never leave with Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would make easier to form a state like that, instead of having a mixed population there. For example, we could not at the time agree on any proposal of Croatian side to have their civilians come back. That would prove the point that they can live together. Even at one of the international meetings it was suggested to -- to form a model village consisting of the Serbs and the Croats living together for a -- better for international community, they could come and see it, yes, they can live together. We were dead against it. And anybody who supported the idea of living ever again together was not welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain a little bit. You talk about the mayor of Vrginmost, Dmitar Obradovic. Can you explain in this context what happened to Mr. Obradovic and why.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic was the mayor in Vrginmost. He was the person that I met once the formation of 21st Corps was completed. And highly intelligent person, a moderate Serb. He was married to a Croatian lady and seems to be very happy in their union. And his general idea for which he fought throughout his being there until his unfortunate demise was that Serbs and Croats can live together and will live together eventually, and we should accept that as a fact. The official Knin was against it. Since they could not remove him in my opinion now, could not remove him by any political means, like having a sudden election for a new mayor or something like that, he would win hands down any way. He was assassinated in the end, and officially we blamed the Croatian side for it. Which kind of -- it makes sense, but we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who, if you know, assassinated Mayor Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ajdinovic was the one who organised the killing itself, and it was done by this Diverzantska Grupa from RSK which were officially part of the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On page 21, you say: "The RSK government, under instructions from Belgrade, had to keep this idea alive of the constant Croatian threat in order to survive." Now, how do you know that it was the instructions from Belgrade to keep this idea alive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The first meeting we had in Belgrade to go for instructions for international negotiations was painfully obvious, that Belgrade doesn't wanted us to reach any settlement. So throughout four to five years, the attitude was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was the attitude?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can't live together. Therefore, we cannot reach any agreement on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you -- you talk in your statement about different tactics that were employed to create what you referred to in the Milosevic case at page 12411 as a psychosis of fear. And some of those tactics you talk about in your statement, the placing of an anti-tank mine between Vrginmost and Glina on the railroad track and placing of mines along the water tower in the vicinity of Glina. Can you describe a little bit of your personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I thought I help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question, just for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe a little bit about what you know about different tactics that were employed to create the psychosis of fear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If the situation in Sector North was too quiet, Belgrade didn't like the idea, because being too quiet usually would lead eventually to some sort of a negotiation and peaceful agreement. As long as we kept tension very high and kept people afraid of supposedly breakthrough the borders by the Croatian army every now and then, their own Diverzantska Grupa would keep population in uniform and a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you give us examples of these types of activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They would pick up an area where something is about to happen, a public meeting of some description. In this instance, about the railway there was a first time that actual train was to go from Vrginmost to Glina since the beginning of the conflict. And they placed an anti-tank line on the railway. So from then on they never attempted it again. The situation about the water tower, again, if you limit people of going anywhere, if you keep people from working field because there's a possibility that somebody has placed mines over there, you are creating a [indiscernible] of fear. People are suddenly very limited where they can go and what they can do, in fear of being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was it that the psychoses of fear -- let me ask it a different way. Who did the RSK want the Serb civilians to be afraid of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with events in Western Slavonia in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The aftermath of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm interested in the aftermath of it. Are you familiar with whether Serbs stayed or left Western Slavonia, after Croatian operations in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was told that no Serbs were left over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know or were you told why Serbs were not left there any longer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That the operation by the Croatian forces very swift and very strong. The Serbs could not defend, they withdrew and with them left the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the civilian population left Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For the same reason they left Knin originally. They were afraid. And if you feed their fears, there is only one possibility and that is to leave the area. Now some of the Croatian army actions helped us a great deal in creating this fear, situation around Medak pocket which is highly advertised throughout the RSK. This is what they are, this is what you can expect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say if you feed their fears, who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Serb population, the civilian population. Not as much armies as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was feeding their fears?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The RSK police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You, at page 26 of your statement, discuss the life of people living in the RSK in 1995. You say: "It seemed as if everyone had gone crazy. People felt trapped in this isolated backwater with no future. Every dispute began being settled with guns." Now, if I could show you a document first. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 1D2602, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile invite the parties to look at page 67, line 7, where apparently the word "no" is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I trust that that is sufficient that you have corrected the record, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is good for our understanding at this moment. Everyone is aware that a lot of work is done on the transcript after the hearing, but I just wanted to verify for myself as well, whether I understood it correctly, because Mr. Lazarevic is telling us a lot of things in a rather quick way, and that causes -- that triggers sometimes the need to verify, and gives our transcriber sometimes a hard time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, this is an article from the Chicago Tribune on January 9, 1995, and you are -- purports to quote you in the article. It talks about guns, violence are cruel rulers of the Krajina frontier, deadly grudges entangle Serbs and Croats. The third paragraph says: "These days the Krajina is controlled by heavily militarised Serbs who, after the ethnic cleansing of about 200.000 Croatians from the area, declared themselves an independent state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please. "Patrons at the UN bar are asked to check their weapons at the door. But in the bar where the Serbs do their drinking, guns are always close at hand. Then it says: "Whether tradition or genetics, it is true that guns always have commanded more respect than governments or laws in the Krajina, in an area that even its Serbian alleys in former Yugoslavia consider to be a particularly violent and scary back water. "Indeed the Krajina in its mountain fastness seems to encapsulates all the darker impulses of the Balkan personality. People are suspicious and clannish. They trust no one but their own. They believe in revenge." If we go towards the middle: "The journalists think we are a bunch of ignorant back-watered gangsters who like killing, said Slobodan Lazarevic, a colonel in the Krajina Serb army who wears a good earring and speaks English with a confidential evidently acquired abroad." Let me ask you, Mr. Lazarevic, did you in fact wear a gold earring in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was a little cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Obviously, you speak English with confidence. Do you recall making this statement to this journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't. Now, at the beginning of article it is mentioning that it is happening in a bar. So somebody passing asked me the question, and I answered the question spontaneously might be it. But it is not the case where I sat down and introduced himself, he said, Look, I produce -- reporter for the Chicago Tribune or whatever. I would like to have a short interview with you. I would refuse it. I would not have it done. So this is a view of the reporter of the things happening in Krajina who has probably been once and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, some of the portions that I have read out there about the culture in 1995, is that in your view consistent with what you said in your statement about every dispute being settled with guns? And in the next paragraph you say the problem was compounded by the total militarization of the population.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The portions that I read out --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- of the article, is that consistent with your view of life in the Krajina in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This is my view of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the article be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: To the extent the witness is quoted, although he can confirm it, on this one we would not have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I -- the Chamber decides to admit it into evidence, it's a kind of a conditional non-objecting. Would then the Chamber expect it to say, Well, under these and these conditions, it is in evidence or not. That makes it a bit problematic because on the one hand side the witness says, I did not give a statement, an interview to this person; but the portions read to him, and that then apparently is his evidence, that that reflects his own views on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I understood, and we can ask the witness, I understood him to say that he doesn't recall giving the statement, but that it's possible that he gave it, and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well, that somebody might have informally have asked him some questions and let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in terms of the probative value, I would also ask that you take into consideration the fact that the reporter provided a description which the witness indicates was accurate at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you are referring to the quotes, because I'm not aware that the witness was given any time to review the whole of the article. I want to be sure about what is evidence, what's not. The portions you put to him, although not formally being interviewed by a journalist, but you may have answered questions that were put to someone, the portions quoted by Mr. Misetic, I understand, reflect your views on the situation at the time. Is that how I have to understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the -- then I think nothing opposes admission into evidence of D1468 anymore, and that it's therefore admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, again, going back to your 1999 witness statement, you say: "This problem was compounded by the total militarization of the population. Every male between 18 and 65 was mobilised, but there were volunteers as young as 16 and as old as 75. Everyone was armed and everyone was required by law to be in uniform all the time, whether they were on duty or not." Now, let me ask you first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide us to the page, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 26, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know in Serbia the ratio of guns to -- guns per person in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The recent article that came out, I read it maybe a week ago is 1.8 per head of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So per head of population in Serbia according to an article you read --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Today, yes. We are 4th in the world by the number of weapons in private possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate, and I know it is not precise and you didn't do a -- a survey. First let me correct something. Line -- or page 73, line 2. No, no, sorry, it's on your screen. You said today we are something in the world. What was the number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you give us a rough estimate --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to clarify, I think Texas is the first on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not from Texas, so ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a rough estimate of how many guns per head were in the Krajina in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At least two per head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would that include civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Two per head, includes everybody. Even the babies, when you take the whole population, number of weapons divided by number of population comes out two per head. So some guy might have five and a six-month-old baby has none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Perhaps get the source of this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I'm interested as well, Mr. Hedaraly, but Mr. Misetic either would ask for it, or you would have done it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. You're give us that number on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the basis by the evidence in writing about the weapons issued to the population within the area of 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of the militarization of the population, was there any difference in terms of population's militarization in Sector South vis-a-vis Sector North?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain, but I would say there is no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were there just regular civilians in the Krajina at the time, to your knowledge, that were not militarised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. There was absolutely no civilian who was really a civilian because everybody -- the concept of defence was taken from the early 1960s in the former Yugoslavia, a concept of Territorial Defence with everybody in the army, everybody defending. I don't think that the Croatians had any different laws at the time anyway. They didn't have to go to the extent, but the rule of such of defending your own country applied to us, at the time. Meaning that everybody who is capable of carrying a weapon will be issued a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about people in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have seen guys with my own eyes with a pair of jeans and a T-shirt and a AK-47 across the shoulder. There's nothing usual about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would the fact that someone was wearing civilian clothes in 1995 mean to you at that time that that person was unarmed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way. On August 6th and 7th, there were a lot of people in civilian carrying weapons, and those were they guys who discarded the RSK uniform, but they kept the weapon with them. Prior to that, there were no civilians, as simple as that, everybody are in the army, excluding ladies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. On page 27 at the top, you say: "I would estimate that all of the Serb losses sustained in the Krajina from 1991 through 1995 over 80 per cent were self-inflicted." What was taking place in the Krajina that that number comes out to 80 percent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, first we have to look at the one important factor to us. Area of Bihac pocket was infused by cash from Arab countries to the tune of 15 billion Deutschemarks and the time, and that was free for taking. Whether it is by trade, whether it is by, I don't know, have a meeting with somebody and have a disagreement and shooting them. But when I refer to the being killed by our own forces or amongst themselves would usually be either setting an old score, disagreement or how to split the spoils from the black market, or somebody had amassed explosive amount of money, so he -- killed him and robbed him, some of less important killings, and two friends are joking around and fulling [sic] by the barrel and the guy had a bullet in the barrel and pulled and it fired and killed him. Instances where the little boy would run up to his father who had an automatic rifle over his shoulder who was fully engaged so he jumped on his father and pulls the trigger accidentally and kills his father so all those are the losses as far as we are concerned military losses, but they cannot be attributed to an enemy attack, so there are losses that happened amongst ourselves. So those are to the height of approximately 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any knowledge of Serb-on-Serb crime taking place during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what type of crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it before, it is rather settling an old score or getting somebody's stash from him. Because you didn't leave that kind of money behind buried because you don't know when you are going to come back; you carry the money with you. Now if two was involved in some black trades over there, and I know you made a quarter of a million Deutschemarks and you probably have it on you right now, the opportunity arises for me to kill you, and I will kill you and take the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But do you know of specific --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only the reports. I didn't witness any of those things, but th reports from Toso Pajic was getting quite worried about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'm going to turn to Operation Storm now. I don't know if you wish to take a break when I change topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise we would take the break in five minutes so this is the best time to -- It was not only in your summary, but you asked the question about the people were obliged by law always to wear a uniform, whereas the evidence that we received until now is that not everyone was always wearing a uniform. Is that piece of legislation something you are going to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can get old Yugoslav legislation. I don't have if I have RSK legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that it was even -- it was in your statement that that there was an obligation that everyone was obliged by law to wear a uniform. Could you guide us as to what specific piece of legislation you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't have it. But what I do have is the orders from my own command. If you conscripted into the army, from then on you are in uniform. And since anybody who is between age of 16 and 60 becomes a part of a military organisation he does carry a uniform and weapon which I say is absolutely everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say, Everyone mobilised, everyone in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break, and we will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One matter has been resolved, Mr. Misetic, that is the broadcast from Courtroom I. Mr. Lazarevic, another matter has not yet been resolved and that is your speed of speech. We'd like to have your testimony as good as can be on our records. If you do not slow down your speed of speech a bit, some of it might be lost, which neither you nor we, nor any of the parties would wish to happen, apart from the hard time out transcriber has.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise again, and I will try to slow it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know, and then will try to give you a sign; that is, when Mr. Misetic doesn't give you a sign. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was reminded during the break, Mr. Lazarevic, perhaps briefly can you explain to us how the black market in Bihac worked. Where is the money coming from, who is trading with whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it earlier, that we estimated approximately 15 billion Deutschemarks floating in Bihac pocket which was the financial aid received by Bosnians from different countries like Emirates, or Saudi Arabia, or whatever, and -- but they were short on supplies of everything else, cigarettes, coffee, fuel. So all of those things were offered by Serbs to them, not in an official capacity. It was not the stand of the government to do it, but individuals would get involved into this black-marketing. I will just give you an example of the existing prices at the time. A packet of cigarettes was 100 Deutschemarks, which people obtained at the airport for 12. A litre of diesel was approximately 15 to 20, depending on the market. I mean, absolutely any food item would be sold there. And you have to consider the closeness of the border between the Bosnia and RSK, so the people living alongside were heavily involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning to Operation Storm, and if we could -- if you look to page 28 of your 1999 statement, you say in the middle of the first paragraph: "Panic set in among the people in Topusko as they realized that there was nothing that could stop the Croatian troops. Everyone knew what had happened to the Croats in the Krajina in 1991 that hundreds had been killed, that all of their homes and businesses had been burned, and that the entire population was forcibly expelled. So there was a universal feeling that when the Croatian army retook the area they would be out for revenge." Now, can you tell us how do you know that this was the universal feeling among the population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By the beginning of the Croatian counterattack or attack, whatever you want to call it, people started sending those who were of the army age, they were sending their families straight to Bosnia or even further to Serbia, so there are already small convoys formed and left the area, very quickly. And those that didn't have anybody down south to go to, when they saw these guys leaving, it triggered a chain reaction. So very quickly it became large convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But my question is: How do you know that people were aware of the crimes that had been committed against Croats and that there was this universal feeling that when the Croatian army retook the area they would be out for revenge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mostly we are dealing here with the local population who had been there for, I don't know, tens of years. And some of the those guys were involved in taking the expelled Croats' property, houses, land, tractors, cars, whatever. So, I don't know. This is how I would feel. If I had done something wrong and the people are coming in, I'm pretty much sure they're going to take it out on me, so I better leave before they come. So that is the feeling that existing among the local population. None of the locals could say, Well, I have not done anything. Well, at least you fired few rounds across the border. We saw this, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up with that. When you say: None of the locals could say, Well, I have not done anything. What do you mean by that, if you could explain that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the conflict that happened in that part of Balkans, everybody re-established that everybody a part of the army structure already. They had been conscripted into the army. By wearing a uniform of the RSK, you were already the enemy of the Croatian army. And so nobody is completely innocent. Nobody could claim, Look, I never took any weapons, I never fired on anybody, I never took anybody's property. I was on my own in my house and I didn't care what was going on around, impossible to claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about women, elderly, why would they leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They're the family members of the people on the front line. Safety reasons, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've discuss at page 27 of your statement, that you had a conversation shortly after the Operation Storm started with a HV liaison officer, named Tihomir, Ticar, Brckan. "He encouraged me and other Serbs in Topusko to stay." Can you tell us first of all where did that conversation -- where were you when that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the UN HQ. I was informed there's a phone call for me there, by the liaison officer from Karlovac which I knew he was -- I think he was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How is it that you wound up in the UN HQ during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was still officially liaison officer, and one of the very important parts of me working at the time was to really protect the UN personnel from any retribution from the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you say in your statement that: "With our headquarters inside the UN base, we had uninterrupted communications capabilities using UN satellite phones."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We did hire an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You hired an office within the UN base?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to remind you again, but we need to pause between my question and your answer. And you say that you paid a Ukrainian sector commander 5.000 Deutschmarks a day as rental for his office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: His deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what did Mr. Brckan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question because I didn't hear it well. You say you paid a Ukrainian ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, at page 27, bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you are quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes: "You secured this office in the UN compound by paying the Ukrainian sector commander 5.000 Deutschemarks a day as rental for his office."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But not the Sector Commander; it was his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is - you reference it in your statement - paid to his Chief of Staff, a Polish colonel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that UN office were you able to communicate with Belgrade, using the UN's phones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apparently they had a satellite connections in the office, so you could call anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let's talk about what the HV liaison officer told you. What did he tell you in that conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a personal contact in my sector on a number of occasions, so we got to know each other quite well. And I believe that he found it in his lack of animosity towards me personally to offer me a save passage through Croatia if I would go to Tusilovic [phoen] in the car with my wife, and he would make certain that nothing happens to me along the way or upon arrival to Croatia. And I should make the same offer to Colonel Bulat, or to anybody else who I meet along the way. It was not the situation when he told me, you know, inform -- inform everybody that this is a standing offer, lay down your weapons, and you will have a safe passage. This an invitation given to me and Colonel Bulat, which I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Bulat is who, at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat was renamed a commanding officer of the 21st Corps at the time. Colonel Bosanac was, up to that point, commanding officer of the 21st Corps was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So when Mr. Brckan offers safe passage to Colonel Bulat, what did you interpret that to mean? Let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's all over. You know, save yourself basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask it a different way. By offering safe passage to Colonel Bulat, did you form an opinion as to whether he was offering safe passage to forces under Colonel Bulat's command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, my personal interpretation of it was if you remove the command, the rest will fall down anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you -- how many days did you hold put, you meaning in the 21st, and Colonel Bulat hold out during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Four to five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So that would put us roughly at August 8th/August 9th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Had you all, in the command, heard that Knin had fallen into HV hands?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First indication that Knin has fallen was given on Croatian TV. That is the first that I have seen the actual Croatian flag fluttering in the wind on the top -- there's castle in Knin. There is a castle in Knin and on top of it was the Croatian flag. And there were a bunch of officers sitting around the TV looking at it and commenting. And I was the one who didn't believe it. I thought, yeah, okay, this is typical Croatian propaganda; it did not happen. I just couldn't accept the fact that Knin could have fallen so easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At some point did you and others in the ARSK command accept the information that, in fact, had fallen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the end, it was unavoidable conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What impact, if any, on the morale of the ARSK did the fall of Knin have?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that too many people knew about it. Those that were informed about it, of course, their morale was an all-time low. Those that didn't know repressed the importance of defending the sector itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification. Mr. Lazarevic, you said at the end it was an unavoidable conclusion. When was that in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Croatian forces came to about 3 kilometres from where we are. So they were deep inside the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be a third day of the attack. We have moved our HQ from where it was, in the vicinity of Vojnic, all the way to the parameter of the UN compound. We out back into the hotel in Topusko. So as the crow flies, we were probably 150 hours [sic] away from the UN compound. And in that circle, which I'd say is a perimeter of approximately 5 kilometres, where there are 4.000 members of the 21st Corps, fully armed, and approximately 20.000 civilians who came in from further south, from Titova Korenica and Slunj, places like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say on the third day, we all know that Operation Storm started, or at least the military operation started at the 4th of August. Now, was it the third day, then, would be the 6th of August. Would that be in the morning hours? Would that be midday? Would that be later that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to explain chronologically what happened at the time. First, you had the -- your main attack had happened early hours of the morning on the 4th. By early afternoon, we are finding out that Knin is no longer our capital city. The following day, we are finding out that two corps, who are were on the left and the right, from the 21st Corps had left the position. That's the Banja Corps and the Lika Corps. On the third day, we had this huge influx ever civilians into Topusko, and from then on it was simply negotiating the way out of this mess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I asked a clarification in relation to your answers given to Mr. Misetic's question, when did you -- when were you informed that Knin had fallen. Then you said, We first saw on television, the flag flying from the castle. We thought this would be propaganda. And, at the end you said, We had to conclude ... So I'm talking about the fall of Knin. Today you also tell me just a second ago, that already on the 4th, you -- I think you said Knin was not our capital anymore. Did you mean to say that you were then aware that Knin had fallen; or if it is not your capital anymore, what ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our sector, in territory of the 21st Corps, we are aware that there is something terribly wrong because we did not have any communication with Sector South anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But again, my question, I mean, I do understand that if the troops are at a distance of just a few kilometres from you and Topusko. But when did you learn that Knin had fallen? That, militarily, Knin was not under ARSK control anymore but, instead, under HV military control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either very late that night or very early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or early in the morning of the 5th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow up on one of your answers to Judge Orie's questions. You said that you knew something was terribly wrong because you didn't have communication anymore with Sector South. Can you describe in a little more detail what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All our calls are unanswered. The only communication we could establish at the time would be by using a phone, and those lines were cut off, or nobody answered it. And that same goes for the police when they tried to get in touch with Knin to find out where Milan Martic is, Toso Pajic, et cetera, they couldn't get through. The military side also couldn't do it. And then we tried to get into touch with, as I said, the Lika Corps or the Banja Corps, and we didn't have communication with them either, and that was the very next day. Which led to us assume that they had withdraw from position without informing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know why or what interrupted your communications with Sector South?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Leading up to Operation Storm, was there a concern among the population about a pending Croatian attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Leading up to Operation Storm, in the days immediately prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is a like a week before, ten days before, six months before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One or two days.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you sense any increased concern about a pending Croatian attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nobody knew about the attack two days before it happened. I found out two days before it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any preparations that were made by RSK authorities about withdrawing the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that would mean that HQ Knin knew about the attack three or four days before it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any concerns amongst the citizens themselves that they would prefer to be withdrawn, if the RSK could not defend itself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Rade Raseta was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Rade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Raseta.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Raseta, I heard the name, but I can't place it right now in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that he worked as an assistant commander for security in the Knin HQ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He might of, But I really can't be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in your statement, talking about the panic among the civilian population, you say that the panic was also fostered - and this is on page 28 of your statement - "the panic was also fostered by Belgrade since they wanted the Serbs to leave the Krajina." You go on to state that: "Belgrade wanted to see Serbs from the Krajina resettled in Kosovo and areas which they felt that they could sustain such as the Serb-held areas in Bosnian and Eastern Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you gave me the page where I made that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 28. Second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What facts led you to that conclusion, that Belgrade wanted the Serbs to loaf the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was always rumour going around, which I have never confirmed it from any official source, that the late President Tudjman and late President Milosevic had made a deal as far as Krajina is concerned. But in this position, I cannot clearly say, yes, that's what happened. I don't know. But this is the general rumour that was going on around. Now development of situation after the attack pointed out that nobody is going to assist us in this defence. And the units on the ground were aware they cannot defend it by the virtual number of attacking force, they cannot defend it, Unless they want to commit a collective suicide. All you had to do is add a little bit of fuel to the fire to make sure that nobody is staying behind because there will be no military left behind to defend the civilian population, if there was any civilian population.
