Now, in my own mind when I look at a situation, the only civilians would be women, children, and really, really, old people. Everybody else, as far as I'm concerned, are of military age, are a part of the military. That is my view of the situation. Analysing the situation, it was painfully obvious that Belgrade has decided, This the end of the road for you guys in Krajina. Do what you can. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you, you talk about on that same page, in the next paragraph: "It was a well orchestrated plan, and those of us in the RSK military and government contracted to the process by intentionally sowing panic among the civilian population." And that paragraph ends: "So a concerted effort was made to frighten people before they had time to see if things would work out. Stories were spread that the Ustashas would kill all the civilians. And I am aware of some individuals actually being tasked with going around to spread stories such as the Ustashas were cutting the throats of children." Can you tell us who these individuals were that were tasked with spreading these stories?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Personally I would place it down to the information ministry in Knin originally. Later on we had a people in convoys coming from further south than our own sector was, who came in with a horrific stories that already happening in the field, on the ground. Stories which were not confirmed, but nobody would like to stay and find out whether they were true or not. Panic is a fast-growing disease. It is very, very difficult to calm masses of people and tell them, This is not what really is not going to happen. All you had to mention certain instances, All right, think what happened to you in 1941, 1945; think what happened to you recently in Medak pocket, think about Maslenica, this about this and that. Does that give you indication is going to finish nicely for you? Even if you had a great deal of imagination working for you, I don't think you would agree, okay, if I stay, nothing is going happen to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, have you dealt with this specific lines or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic, looking at your statement, you are talking about people being tasked to spread these stories. Now, when Mr. Misetic asked you who were tasked with that, you said, well, in the beginning of the ministry of information. And then you told us a lot about rumours and stories which were not verified and people would not take the risk that they might be true. Now, there is a, for me, a huge difference between tasking people and say, You tell this story, you tell that story, you spread this -- intentionally, you spread this panic, compared to people telling each other the worse things that had happened. So what you told us after you talked about the Ministry of Information was not tasking people to spread false rumours. Is there any other example you could give us where people were specifically tasked - so another from the ministry of Information. So I'm not talking about how rumours spread but whether you are aware of persons specifically tasked to promote spreading rumours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was -- I can't remember the name unfortunately. But there was a priest, so there couldn't be too many of those in the Slunj area who was asked to explain to people why they need to leave. So, to me, he is given a task to prepare for the evacuation from Slunj area. This is something I have found out later on, not during the actual happenings. To anybody that I spoke to, it was always there's nothing to wait for. We got to leave as quickly as possible. And that was on the level of the command all the way down to the -- to political structures in the Sector North. Nobody actually encouraged us to stay. But everybody encouraged to us leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, sir, that you are asking for a specific question, if somebody is given a task, do I no who is giving the task and by whom. That I don't know. I know there were people who are just going around telling to leave, telling others to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now about the priest, do you know who asked him to tell the people why they had to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was he was asked directly by Milan Martic to prepare civilian population to leave. Why they picked Slunj, whether this was a directive given to the other priests in others areas, I don't know. Specifically this instance, I know. At the same time, there was this letter going around apparently, supposedly signed by Milan Martic saying that all civilians should be evacuated from the RSK. And I place down about 50 per cent of the people say, No, no, no, no, it is fabricated, and another 50 percent say, Good thing he told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said your understanding was that it was Milan Martic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- who addressed this priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On what was this understanding based? Talking about the people after we actually met in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is not perfectly clear. Do you intend to say that you heard about this later, when you were in Belgrade? That it was Mile Martic that would have asked that priest ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So-called government in exile from RSK was given by the Serbian politicians, if you like, offices in the middle of Belgrade. So if anybody knows Belgrade, it's Mose Pijade Street, number 2 on the fourth floor, which consists of about 20 to 30 offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave the details apart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who told you it was Mile Martic that asked this priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People very close to the priest, whether it be Mile Bosnic, who I know personally before the conflict, and he was in Slunj at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- I didn't catch the name. You said whether it would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mile Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bosnic, yes. So you heard it from circles close to the priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Close to the priest or close to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Lazarevic, who was Mile Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Appointments in RSK at the time were changed every so often. You went to bed as ministry of energy, and you wake up as ministry of information; this type of situation. Bosnic was politically involved on the government level in Knin. He was a minister of something. But I'm not quite sure right now, minister of what. Could it be a minister without portfolio, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what happened in Petrova Gora during Operation Storm? And first if you could tell us where Petrova Gora is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Petrova Gora is approximately -- it is a national park. I don't know what it is today. At the time it was a national park. There was a military installation there which we had our own HQ at the time, the 21st Corps, and then appearance of the special units of police from Belgrade, we needed to move away from there, and that's where Frenki had his HQ. And from then on it was off limits to us, the military part of RSK or the 21st Corps. So it was their own HQ at the time of the attack on the morning of the 4th. Within day or two of the attack, we have sent a patrol to Petrova Gora to see what is going on over there. The place was deserted and set on fire. So no police presence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to how it was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we believe they did it themselves. Upon withdrawal they decided to destroy everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who is they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The special police, Frenki and his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you also in your statement talk about conversations that took place from the UN facility between Colonel Bulat and Momcilo Perisic, and then there was conversations with Jovica Stanisic, and Mr. Lilic from your location in the UN HQ with them. What was the message they were sending you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They all repeated exactly the same thing, and it was one word "persevere" without any further elaboration on it or promise of assistance, or -- I have to say that at the time we still believed that some sort of assistance would be offered by Serbia and by the Republika Srpska in Bosnia. Because they claimed they will send an air force to help us out, warranties are on the way on the busses, and things like that, which are all unconfirmed. But we had this meeting in the UN HQ, in the office that we used, when those people that you mentioned - Colonel Bulat, Toso Pajic was the minister of interior at the time - [indiscernible] was there, I was there, and they used the inter-phone when they spoke to these people. So they would -- Toso Pajic, if he is going to call Stanisic, we would hear from the bell to the conclusion of conversation, everything. And basically what happened is a commanding officer of the 21st Corps, Colonel Bulat, would report on the situation to General Perisic and tell him, This is where we are. This is -- we are encircled. This is what we are facing on our own, nothing much we can do right now. What do you suggest, General? The answer was persevere, and click. Exactly the same thing would be -- with Jovica Stanisic when Toso Pajic spoke to him, again he would explain the situation more or less the same way that Colonel Bulat just did five minutes before. Again the answer we got is persevere, and click, meaning the other party has cut off the line. And the political side of it, okay, let's see what Lilic has to say about it. It was the same thing. We looked at each other in the office, and we were under impression that these people are sitting exactly in the same office somewhere and looked at each other and said, Oh, just tell them persevere. Because it is uncanny how they use the same word without any further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you all, on the ARSK side, reach any conclusions on the basis of what you were being told, that is, to persevere?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the persevere could only be translated into one thing, is keep fighting and something good will come out of it. All was sitting in the office knew. This is a battle we cannot win. Obviously we're being sacrificed. Why we think we are sacrificed? Because the movement of the corps on the left flank and right flank withdrew from a position without telling us meant we are left there with reason, and the reason was not because the 21st Corps was the ultimate fighting force on Balkan. Oh, we could take anybody now. They are simple people. So there is -- tried to explain to each other why is this done? And then the conclusion came by itself, that the Belgrade wants some cheap points. Cheap points to the tune of 5.000 people, or 20.000 people. I never believed that the Croats would walk in and kill everybody. I did not believe myself. I don't think Toso Pajic believed it. I don't think Bulat believed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we need to clarify what you mean by "cheap points." What do you mean Belgrade wanted cheap points?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will use expression which I did not use in the original statement. They wanted to make Srebrenica out of Topusko. In this case, it was Croatian side to be blamed for. So the idea was to present it to the world, in this world nobody smelled roses. They are just as bad as we are. Say they just killed bunch of civilians in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, at page 30 of your statement, you say in the first full paragraph: "With the climate of fear that had been maintained over the preceding four years, and with all of the scare tactics used after the Croatian offensive was launched, there were very few Serbs willing to stay in Topusko?" And then on page 33, at the top, you say: "In any event," -- and you have made this correction, so I'll skip that word. But: "In any event, people were so terrorised by their own government's propaganda that few would have risked staying in Croatia." Explain to us what you mean by those two statements, in terms of the propaganda over four years and few people being willing to stay in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think we touched that before, about the maintaining the tension within the RSK on purpose. At a later stages, if a commander of a battalion would walk amongst these men and say, Folks, get your families out of here, we will stay and fight, but get your family to safety, situation like that, I don't think anybody is prepared to stay. And even those who are in uniform would try to leave. They would be a lot of desertion, people just throwing away the uniform and hopping in a car, or whatever transport they have, and just walk away. At that particular point in time, we didn't want that every person of military age would just simply leave. Maybe at the back of our mind we hoped that will somehow prevail. Obviously we were wrong. But maintaining this tension throughout the existence of RSK was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this specific question. You've testified that in this pocket where you were encircled during Operation Storm, I believe you said there were 5.000 ARSK troops and 20.000 civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Explain to us, why didn't the military - in other words, why didn't the 5.000 soldiers - withdraw to Serbia but the 20.000 civilians stay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure I quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why didn't the 20.000 civilians -- let me take a step back. Your situation up in Sector North with Colonel Bulat was negotiated peacefully with the HV; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat surrendered to General Stipetic of the HV; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the HV allowed your forces passage to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: With civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking first about the military.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your -- ARSK military was allowed by Croatia to travel from Sector North through Western Slavonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All the way to Eastern Slavonia and into Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for us why the 20.000 civilians also went with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were not from Topusko. They would be left in the middle of somewhere that didn't even live. The development of the situation of what's going around it, didn't encourage them to say. It was a way out. Specifically, we getting report that 5th Corps is attacking the convoys down south trying to cross into the Republika Srpska. Nobody would want to go there. So it was very important to us to negotiate the withdrawal through Croatia, which eventually we did. But it was not only soldiers but the civilians within the Topusko area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what impact, if any, did this four years of fear have on the decision of the civilians to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A great deal, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You guess --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If you're under constant pressure by your own government, that -- this is a very unnatural way of live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, being in a conflict itself which is not resolved, and sooner or later the Croats will try to re-take the territory. You better be ready for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to your arrival in Serbia, what happened in terms of the highway when you got over the Serbian border? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From the moment I eventually crossed the border, even though I was the seventh car in convoy, by the time we reached the area of Sid which is the crossing between Croatia and Serbia proper, I was asked to stay behind with a couple of officers from the Croatian army and take the names of the people crossing in a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You said -- you were asked -- with -- to take the names with officers of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or the Croatian police, one of the -- people in uniforms, Croatian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just -- briefly just in a notebook write down the names of the people crossing. Not asking them the rank, don't ask them which units they belonged to, just make a certain evidence that they did cross. And that took me about, I don't know, 25, 30 hours. And when the last person crossed, that's when I crossed. The moment I crossed, I parked the car and slept for about 10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you talk about seeing Serbian police activity directing people to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By the time I felt fresh enough to continue my journey, I was entering the Sid area, and there was already ramp made there, and actually I caught up with the end of the convoy, so obviously it is taking too long for people to cross. And they were all searched, including my car, and I was rather annoyed. I said, We just drove through Croatia for a number of kilometres, and nobody searched us and yet, I'm coming home, and you want me to take everything out of my car, and line it up on a road so you can see what is in there. The guy had apologetic kind of sound to him, saying, well, he was ordered to do this. It is not his idea; so, okay. Sorry, guys. So I actually had to do search. And once I managed to cross, this was still the road which is leading from the old Brotherhood and Unity highway from Croatia going all the way down to Nis and beyond. It's a highway with its own exits, every now and then, and all those exits were blocked by a police, the Serbian police, the regular police, not special units or anything like that. Special police with rotation on blocking the road and saying, No, you cannot leave the highway. You have to stay on the highway and move south. Now, to me, south simply meant Kosovo. Why would they send tens of thousands of people to Nis? Probably -- if they cannot be absorbed in Belgrade, they're not going to be absorbed in Nis either, or Kragujevac. So they will have to continue all the way south, and to most of us, south meant Kosovo. So as I was -- I was driving a bit faster than the rest of the convoy that I caught up with, I left them behind, and yet I did not reach the end tail of the convoy that came in first. So there was one section of the road totally deserted. I came to the road which is leaving the highway, and there was a police car parked there but there was nobody in attendance, so I just swerved around and went -- went -- I'm sorry, I keep waving my arms. There was nobody in attendance there. So actually, I got off the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can ask one quick question or we can finish for the day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the length of the answers, I would rather have that question put to the witness tomorrow. Mr. Lazarevic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II, and I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether you have given that testimony already, or whether it is still to be given; doesn't make any difference. Could the usher escort Mr. Lazarevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would just like to inquire with you, the witness has been scheduled for six hours. You're at three and a half now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will be finished within half an hour tomorrow, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within half an hour, that's -- Well, then, perhaps it is useless to give you further guidance as to try to keep the answers a bit short, and -- because the witness tends to move on from a simple absolutely to longer answers. We adjourn until tomorrow, the 3rd of June, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
